questions_and_answers.answer: Answer When the Federal Reserve (Fed) raises its target interest rate, it typically does so by selling government bonds in open-market operations. This reduces the money supply in the economy, as the public buys these bonds. Money Market Changes In the money market graph, the money supply curve (MS) would shift to the left, representing a decrease in the money supply. The new equilibrium point would be at a higher interest rate (due to the Fed's target increase) and a lower quantity of money. MS (after Fed's policy) = MS (before Fed's policy) - Quantity of money sold by the Fed Aggregate Demand Changes The increase in the interest rate makes borrowing more expensive. This discourages residential and business investment spending, leading to a decrease in the aggregate demand. The aggregate demand curve would shift to the left, indicating a lower quantity of output demanded at each price level.
